chunks: "I'd group the reasons into four buckets. First, manufacturing defects : solder bridges, opens, tombstoned resistors, cold joints, or BGA joints that didn't wet.
Even a very low defect rate adds up when a board has thousands of joints. Second, design errors : wrong footprint, flipped pinout, a missing pull-up, a layout mistake.
These show up in prototypes and are the main reason for bodge wires and part swaps in bring-up.
Third, component problems : a part damaged by ESD or overstress, a bad lot, an out-of-spec or counterfeit part, or something that failed in test or in the field.
And fourth, changes : a spec change after boards are built, a part going obsolete, or firmware wanting a different configuration.
Which one it is matters, because the response is different. Assembly defects point at the paste stencil, the footprint, or the reflow profile.
Design errors point at review and checklists. Component issues point at supply chain and handling.
If I see the same rework in the same spot repeatedly, I treat it as a design or process problem and fix that, not just rework it again."
